source_text: ἐκτετίμηται δὲ μᾶλλον τὸ ἀμωμήτως ἔχον, καὶ νοσοῦν οὐδαμόθεν τὴν παραφθορὰν, ἄρτιον δὲ ὥσπερ εἰς ἀρετὴν, καὶ εὐσθενὲς εἰς ἁγιασμὸν, τὸ εὐδοκιμεῖν εὖ μάλα μεμελετηκὸς ἐν ὑπομονῇ, καὶ γοργὸν εἰς σύνεσιν διηνεκῆ. Τοιγαροῦν καὶ κατὰ παντὸς ἰόντα τοῦ γένους τὸν ἐπὶ τῷδε ποιεῖται νόμον, ἀκίβδηλον ἑαυτῷ τὸ ἱερὸν καὶ ἀπόλεκτον ἀποφαίνων γένος· τότε μὲν ὡς ἐν φυλῇ τῇ Λευῒ, καὶ ὡς ἐξ αἵματος Ἀαρὼν, νυνί γε μὴν ὡς ἔν γε τοῖς ἡγιασμένοις ἐν Χριστῷ τῷ μεγάλῳ καὶ κατ' ἀλήθειαν ἀρχιερεῖ, ᾧ προσπεφύκαμεν διὰ πνεύματος, κοινωνοὶ καὶ μέτοχοι τῆς οἰκείας αὐτοῦ φύσεως ἀναδεδειγμένοι. Τοιγάρτοι καὶ εἰς ἀδελφότητα κεκληκὼς τοὺς ἐν πίστει δεδικαιωμένους, ὥσπερ κοινωνοῖς αὐτοῖς ἐπαγάλλεται λέγων· «Ἰδοὺ ἐγὼ καὶ τὰ παιδία ἅ μοι ἔδωκεν ὁ Θεός.» Ἢ γὰρ οὐχὶ τῷ προσώπῳ Χριστοῦ καὶ τὸν ἐπὶ τῷδε λόγον ἀνάπτειν ἐδόκει τῶ θεσπεσίῳ Παύλῳ; {ΠΑΛΛ.} Πάνυ μὲν οὖν. {ΚΥΡ.} Ἀπείργει δὴ οὖν τοῦ ἱερᾶσθαι δεῖν τὸν ἐφ' ὅτῳ οὖν τῶν ὠνομασμένων, ὡς ἄῤῥωστον καὶ κατεσκωμμένον. Οὐ γὰρ προσελεύσεται, φησὶ, προσφέρειν τὰ δῶρα τοῦ Θεοῦ, ἄνθρωπος τυφλὸς ἢ χωλός. Ἔχει μὲν οὖν αὐτόθεν, κἂν εἰ νοοῖτο σωματικῶς, πολὺ τὸ χρῆμα τὸ ἀκαλλές· ἐξεῤῥυηκότοιν γὰρ ὀφθαλμοῖν, καὶ μὴν καὶ ποδὸς οὐκ ἐρηρεισμένου, ὀρθὰ βαίνειν οὐκ ἔχοντος, πῶς οὐκ ἄμεινον ἠρεμεῖν, οὐδὲ ὅποι ποτὲ ἰέναι χρὴ τὸν ἱερέα διεγνωκότα, ἤγουν ἰέναι σὺν γέλωτι, ποδί τε καὶ ὀφθαλμοῖς ἀλλοτρίοις χρώμενον; Ἀλλ' εἴη μὲν ἂν οὐ πολὺς ὁ τοῦδε λόγος. Τὰ δ' ἀναγκαῖα πρὸς γνῶσιν καὶ θεωρίαν ἡμῖν τὴν πνευματικὴν, φέρε λέγωμεν, τὸ τῆς ἱστορίας ὑποτρέχοντες παχύ. Τυφλὸν μὲν οὖν ἔοικε τὸν εὐήθη λίαν καὶ ἀνούστατον ἀποκαλεῖν. Ὃ γάρ ἐστιν ὀφθαλμὸς τῷ γηΐνῳ σώματι, τοῦτο καὶ ἐν ψυχῇ λέγοιτ' ἂν ὁ νοῦς, φωτὶ μὲν τῷ θείῳ καταλαμπόμενος, καὶ πρὸς αὐτὸ τὸ ἀκήρατον ἀναμύων κάλλος, καὶ ταῖς τῶν ἐννοιῶν ἰσχναῖς οἱονεί πως καὶ εὐστρόφοις κινήσεσιν ἀναθρώσκων εὖ μάλα πρὸς τὸ ἀκριβὲς ἐν δόξῃ, καὶ δογματικῆς ὀρθότητος οὐχ ἁμαρτάνειν εἰδώς. Τοῦτο, οἶμαι, ἐστὶ τὸ παροιμιωδῶς εἰρημένον, «Οἱ ὀφθαλμοί σου ὀρθὰ βλεπέτωσαν, τὰ δὲ βλέφαρά σου νευέτω δίκαια.» Εἴρηται δέ που καὶ πρὸς τὴν τῶν Ἰουδαίων μητέρα βλέπουσαν οὐκ ὀρθῶς· «Ἰδοὺ οὐκ εἰσὶν οἱ ὀφθαλμοί σου, οὐδὲ ἡ καρδία σου καλὴ, ἀλλ' ἢ εἰς τὴν πλεονεξίαν σου καὶ εἰς τὸ αἷμα τὸ ἀθῶον ἐκχέειν αὐτὸ, καὶ εἰς τὰ ἀδικήματά σου, καὶ εἰς φόνον τοῦ ποιεῖν αὐτά.» Ἀνεπιτήδειος οὖν εἰς ἱερουργίαν ὁ τυφλὸς νοητῶς, τοῦτ' ἔστιν ὁ παντελῶς ἀσύνετος, καὶ νοῦν καὶ φρένα λελωβημένος. Ἀνεπιτήδειος δὲ πρὸς τούτῳ καὶ ὁ χωλὸς, τοῦτ' ἔστιν ἀνὴρ ὀρθοποδεῖν οὐκ εἰδὼς, καὶ πρὸς τὸ ἀρτίως βαίνειν οὐκ εὐσθενής. Ἡ μὲν γὰρ τυφλότης, καθάπερ ἔφην ἀρτίως, τῆς εἰς ἄκρον ἀσυνεσίας σύμβολον· χωλότης δὲ αὖ, τῆς οἱονεὶ κεκλασμένης καὶ ἀδρανοῦς κινήσεώς τε καὶ προθυμίας, ἣν ἂν ἐφ' ἑκάστῳ ποιοῖτό τις τυχὸν τῶν πρακτέων. Εἰ μὴ τοῖς οὕτω λελωβημένοις ἐπιφωνεῖν ἄξιον·
pass_a_gloss: [cont.] but rather prized (ἐκτιμάω, pf.) is what is blameless, and in no way sick with corruption (παραφθορά), complete (ἄρτιος) as toward virtue and strong (εὐσθενής) toward sanctification (ἁγιασμός), having practised (μελετάω) very well to be approved (εὐδοκιμέω) in endurance (ὑπομονή), and vigorous (γοργός) toward continual understanding (σύνεσις διηνεκής). Therefore he makes the law on this going against the whole family, showing the sacred and chosen race unalloyed (ἀκίβδηλος) for himself: then as in the tribe of Levi and from the blood of Aaron, but now as in those sanctified in Christ the great and truly High Priest (ἀρχιερεύς), to whom we have grown onto (προσφύω) through the Spirit, shown as sharers and partakers (κοινωνοὶ καὶ μέτοχοι) of his own (οἰκεία) nature (φύσις). So, having called into brotherhood (ἀδελφότης) those justified (δικαιόω) in faith, as over partners he exults (ἐπαγάλλομαι) saying: ‘Behold, I and the children whom God gave me.’ Or did it not seem good to divine Paul to attach (ἀνάπτω) this word to the person (πρόσωπον) of Christ? PALL.: Altogether so. CYR.: He shuts out (ἀπείργω) from needing to act as priest the one [afflicted] with whichever of the named, as sick and mocked (κατασκώπτω). For he shall not approach, it says, to offer the gifts of God, a blind or lame man. It has, then, from itself, even if understood bodily (σωματικῶς), much unseemliness (ἀκαλλές); for with eyes run out (ἐκρέω) and foot not firmly planted (ἐρείδω), not able to walk straight, how is it not better to stay quiet (ἠρεμέω), the priest not even discerning where he must go, or to go with laughter using alien (ἀλλότριος) foot and eyes? But the account of this would not be long. What is necessary for knowledge (γνῶσις) and spiritual contemplation (θεωρία πνευματική), come, let us say, running beneath the thickness (παχύ) of the history (ἱστορία). Blind he seems to call the very simple (εὐήθης) and most senseless (ἀνούστατος). For what the eye is to the earthy body, this in the soul would be called mind (νοῦς), illumined (καταλάμπω) by the divine light and opening eyes (ἀναμύω) to the pure (ἀκήρατος) beauty itself, and with the slender and, as it were, nimble (εὔστροφος) motions of thoughts (ἔννοιαι) leaping up (ἀναθρώσκω) toward exactness in opinion (δόξα), and knowing not to miss doctrinal rightness (δογματικὴ ὀρθότης). This is what is said proverbially: ‘Let your eyes look straight; let your eyelids nod (νεύω) just things.’ And it was said to the mother of the Jews, not seeing straight: ‘Behold, your eyes are not, nor your heart good, but only toward your greed (πλεονεξία), and toward innocent blood to pour it out, and toward your wrongs, and toward murder to do them.’ Unfit (ἀνεπιτήδειος) for sacred service (ἱερουργία), then, is the intelligibly (νοητῶς) blind, i.e., the wholly unintelligent (ἀσύνετος), maimed (λωβάομαι) in mind and wit (φρήν). Unfit too the lame, i.e., a man not knowing to walk straight (ὀρθοποδέω) and not strong to step soundly. For blindness, as I said, is symbol (σύμβολον) of utmost unintelligence; lameness of the as-it-were broken (κλάω) and feeble (ἀδρανής) motion and eagerness (προθυμία) one might make toward each of the things to be done (πρακτέα). Unless it is worthy to cry out (ἐπιφωνέω) to those so maimed: [cont. §4]
pass_b_english: Cyril: …rather, what he holds in honor is the blameless: what suffers no corruption from any quarter, what is sound, so to speak, in virtue and strong in sanctification, what has trained itself thoroughly to win approval through patient endurance, and is always quick to understand. That is why he makes his law on this point extend to the whole family, showing the sacred and chosen race to be his own and free of all alloy: then, in the tribe of Levi and the blood of Aaron; but now in those who have been sanctified in Christ, the great and true High Priest (Hebrews 4:14), to whom we have been joined through the Spirit, and so have been shown to be sharers and partakers of his own nature (2 Peter 1:4). So too, having called into brotherhood those who have been justified by faith (Hebrews 2:11), he rejoices over them as sharers with him, saying: ‘Here am I, and the children whom God has given me’ (Hebrews 2:13; Isaiah 8:18). Or did not the inspired Paul see fit to attach this saying, too, to the person of Christ?

Cyril: He bars from serving as priest, then, anyone with any of the defects named, as infirm and open to ridicule. For it says, ‘A man who is blind or lame shall not come near to offer the gifts of God’ (Leviticus 21:17–18). Now even taken in a bodily sense, the matter plainly has much that is unseemly. For when the eyes have wasted away, and the foot is not firm and cannot walk straight, is it not better for the priest to keep still, since he cannot even tell where he ought to go, rather than to go about amid laughter, using another’s foot and another’s eyes? But we need not say much about that. Let us rather speak of what we need for knowledge and spiritual contemplation, getting beneath the coarse surface of the history. By ‘blind,’ then, he seems to mean the man who is very foolish and utterly senseless. For what the eye is to the earthly body, the mind may be called in the soul. It is lit up by the divine light, it opens its eyes to that pure beauty itself, and with the fine and nimble movements, as it were, of its thoughts it springs up readily toward exact belief, and knows how to keep from missing right doctrine. This, I think, is what is said in the Proverbs: ‘Let your eyes look straight, and let your eyelids nod toward what is just’ (Proverbs 4:25). And somewhere it is also said to the mother of the Jews, who did not see rightly: ‘See, your eyes are not good, nor is your heart; they are set on nothing but your greed, on innocent blood, to shed it, on your wrongdoings, and on murder, to commit them’ (Jeremiah 22:17). So the one who is blind in the spiritual sense is unfit for sacred service, that is, the man wholly without understanding, maimed in mind and judgment. Unfit as well is the lame man, that is, one who does not know how to walk uprightly and has no strength to walk soundly. For blindness, as I said just now, is a sign of utter lack of understanding; lameness, in turn, is a sign of a movement and eagerness that is, as it were, broken and feeble, such as a man may show toward each of the things he has to do. Unless it is right to call out to those so maimed:

anf_compare.notes: No public-domain English of Cyril De adoratione Book 12 exists. Translated fresh from the PG 68 Greek on 2026-10-23; the earlier English of this book was not used as a base.

apparatus.note: PG OCR; column may cut mid-sentence.

PG 68.785. ‘Great … High Priest’ echoes Hebrews 4:14 (ἀρχιερέα μέγαν); ‘sharers … of his own nature’ echoes 2 Peter 1:4 (κοινωνοὶ φύσεως); ‘called into brotherhood’ echoes Hebrews 2:11 just before the quoted Hebrews 2:13 (itself from Isaiah 8:18): all cited. ‘Chosen race’ (ἀπόλεκτον γένος) may echo 1 Peter 2:9, but Cyril’s word differs (ἐκλεκτόν there): left uncited. ‘Spirit’ (διὰ πνεύματος) read as the Holy Spirit, by Cyril’s usual teaching on union with Christ. Cyril takes Hebrews as Paul’s. Proverbs 4:25 has the same number in LXX and English. Jeremiah 22:17 in context is addressed to the king (Jehoiakim/Shallum); Cyril reads it as said to ‘the mother of the Jews’ (Jerusalem): kept as he has it. ὀρθοποδεῖν (‘walk uprightly’) may echo Galatians 2:14, but the passage is about the lameness type, so left uncited. ἤγουν in the laughter sentence read as comparative (‘rather than’). The sentence ending ‘call out to those so maimed:’ leads into the Isaiah quotation that opens §4.
